Seven lenders cut investor borrowing power by up to 20%. Nobody sent you a letter.
What changed
In the May Budget the government said rental losses on established property bought after 12 May 2026 stop offsetting your wages from 1 July 2027. New builds are exempt.
Why your bank cares
For years lenders added the tax benefit of a rental loss back into your income when they assessed you. If the concession is going, so is the add-back.
Three columns
Before: tax saving added back to income · Now: assessed on the cash shortfall alone · Result: up to 20% less borrowing on some calculators

The nine in ten investors with one or two properties, buying the next one this spring. Same job, same rent, smaller number.
The trade-off
The new number is more honest. It's what the property actually costs you each month. Not a bad thing to know before you bid.

slots.title: The bank's favourite structure
slots.hook: The bank's favourite loan structure is the one that costs you the most.
slots.angle: Deal breakdown, de-identified composite. A client came in with a home and an investment property on one facility with one bank. Cross-collateralisation ties every property to every loan. script.setup: Desk plus a second angle 30 to 40 degrees off, Lane B. Outfit 2. Clap at the top of each take, cut to B on every point.
script.spoken:
The bank's favourite loan structure is the one that costs you the most.

It's called cross-collateralisation, and most people who have it don't know they have it.

Here's how it happens. You own your home. You buy an investment property. The bank offers to lend against both together. One facility, one application, less paperwork. Sounds helpful.

Now here's what you actually signed.

Every property secures every loan. The bank has a claim over the lot.

Sell one, and the bank revalues everything before it lets go. If values have dipped, it can hold your sale proceeds to fix up the loan on the one you kept.

Want to refinance one property to a better lender? You can't. They come as a set.

And every valuation, every top-up, runs through one credit team's view of your whole position.

The alternative is ring-fencing. Each property, its own loan. Use equity from one as a cash deposit on the next, but keep the securities separate.

The trade-off is real. More paperwork, sometimes two sets of fees, and it takes a broker willing to do the work instead of ticking the bank's box.

But you keep your options. And over ten years, options are worth more than convenience.

script.spoken:
Fixing your rate is buying insurance from the person who sets the price.

Over a full cycle, variable has beaten fixed almost every time. The bank prices the fixed rate, and the bank is not in the business of losing that bet.

Right now the best fixed rates sit above the best variable ones. So fixing today isn't a discount. It's a hedge.

And a hedge is fine, if you know that's what you're buying.

Who it's right for: the borrower who genuinely couldn't hold another rise.

Certainty has a price. Just know you're paying it.

slots.title: Does my HECS debt matter?
slots.hook: Your HECS debt is costing you more borrowing power than your car loan.
slots.angle: Client question this week. Lenders treat the compulsory repayment as a fixed monthly outgoing, scaled to your income band, so a five-figure balance can knock six figures off capacity. New this year: some lenders can ignore a HELP debt that will be cleared within about a year. Trade-off: paying it out of your deposit can leave you short on deposit. It is a trade, not a rule.

script.spoken:
Your HECS debt is costing you more borrowing power than your car loan.

A client asked this week whether a forty thousand dollar balance mattered. It matters more than the number suggests.

Lenders don't look at what you owe. They look at the repayment coming out of your pay, and they treat it like a loan you can't cancel.

On a typical calculator, that's six figures off what you can borrow.

Two things changed this year. Some lenders can now ignore a balance you'll clear within about a year. And paying it out of your deposit can leave you short on deposit.

It's a trade, not a rule.

The wrong model
Most people think fixed rates follow the cash rate. They don't. Variable rates track the cash rate. Fixed rates don't.

What the market thinks the RBA will do over the next one to five years. That view changes daily, on inflation data, jobs numbers, and what happens overseas.

By the time a decision is announced, fixed rates have usually already moved. You're not getting ahead of anything by fixing the day before.

Buying certainty. It is not a bet you win if rates rise. It's insurance, and insurance has a premium.

Most fixed loans take away your offset and cap your extra repayments. If you might sell, refinance or pay it down hard, that costs more than the rate difference.

Fix because you can't handle a rise. Not because you think you've timed it.

script.spoken:
Property one was easy. Property two was fine. Property three is where most people stop, and nobody warned them it was coming.

Here's what changes.

Your rental income gets shaded. The bank counts 70 to 80 cents of every rent dollar, because of vacancy and costs. So on paper, every property you own costs you more than it does in real life.

Then your existing loans get assessed at about 3% above what you're actually paying. Your own portfolio is now the thing blocking you.

Add a debt to income cap on top and the maths stops working while your bank statements look fine.

Almost everyone in this position thinks the answer is to earn more.

It usually isn't. What actually moves it is which lender you go to, because the shading and the assessment rates are not the same everywhere. Whether your loans are tangled together or kept separate. And whether anybody has looked at the whole portfolio at once, instead of one application at a time.

They live where they want to live. They invest where the numbers work. Those are allowed to be two different places.

The most common reason a settlement slips has nothing to do with the bank's decision.
It's the insurance certificate
Before settlement, your lender needs a building insurance policy that names them as an interested party. Not a quote. Not a screenshot. The certificate.
Why they want it
They're about to hand over a large sum secured by a building. If it burns down uninsured, they own a fire-damaged block of land.
Why it goes wrong
People buy the policy and forget the lender has to be listed on it. Or the sum insured is too low. Or the start date is after settlement.
The other classic
A wrong digit in a bank account number. Surplus funds bounce, and everyone waits while it's traced.
What to do
Get the policy the day you get loan documents. Send the certificate straight through. Check the lender's name and the start date yourself.
Close
Nobody loses a settlement over the loan. They lose it over a PDF.

slides: Cover
The approval came through. Then the number needed to change. Here's what that actually costs.
What happened
Formally approved. Then the required amount went up, so the file went back to the lender for a higher figure.
It's not a re-application
The assessment already exists. It's a variation. But it goes back into a queue, and the queue doesn't care that you were approved yesterday.
What gets re-checked
Servicing at the new amount. The valuation against the new LVR. Sometimes the lender's mortgage insurance position, which can change the cost.
What it costs
Days, mostly. New loan documents get issued, which means signing again, which means the settlement date moves if it was tight.
How to avoid it
Get approved for the number you might actually need, not the number you hope to pay. Room at the top is free. Going back for it isn't.
Close
Being approved isn't the end of the process. It's the start of a different one.
